title: The seven churches of Rome
hookLine: Philip Neri's walking pilgrimage with picnics and songs

cards: Early morning in Rome, centuries ago. A crowd gathers around a priest known for jokes as much as for prayer: shopkeepers, students, a few nobles, some boys from the streets. They set off on foot together, singing.
They stop at one great church, pray, and walk on to the next. Midday, they sit down in a garden and eat lunch together: bread, wine, cheese, fruit.
Then musicians play, and the crowd walks on, church after church, until evening. The priest is Philip Neri, and this day has a name.

teach.b: The visit to the seven churches is an old Roman pilgrimage: one long day's walk to seven of the city's great churches.
Saint Peter's. Saint Paul Outside the Walls. Saint John Lateran.
Saint Mary Major. Saint Lawrence Outside the Walls. Holy Cross in Jerusalem.
Saint Sebastian, by the catacombs. Pilgrims made this round before Philip; tradition says he turned it into something crowds could join. You met Philip in year three.
He's remembered as the saint of joy, and stories about him are full of jokes, odd hats and teasing, which, the stories say, kept him and others from taking themselves too seriously. Why a walk?

teach.h: A BETTER DAY OUT THAN CARNIVAL.
teach.b: Tradition says Philip led these walks partly as a cheerful alternative to the rowdiness of carnival season. Instead of telling people what not to do, he gave them a better day out. And why the picnic?
This is the surprise. A pilgrimage could have been grim and silent.

teach.h: THE PICNIC IS PART OF THE PRAYER.
teach.b: Philip made eating together part of it, so sitting on the grass with strangers became part of the prayer, not a break from it.
The Psalms, in the Douay-Rheims: "Behold how good and how pleasant it is for brethren to dwell together in unity." Good, and pleasant. Both words.
Last, the walk is still made. Parishes and groups in Rome keep the custom, and pilgrims trace the route on foot. The churches are far apart, the feet get tired, and the lunch still tastes good.

how: Pilgrims in Rome walk the route of the seven churches in a single day, praying in each; some parishes and groups keep Philip Neri's custom of making it together, with music and a shared meal on the way.

games.q: you're Philip Neri. carnival season is coming, and the young people of Rome are heading for the rowdy streets. what do you do?
o: preach a hard sermon against carnival.
lead them on a long walk to the churches, with music and lunch.
stay home and pray for them.
games.why: tradition says he gave them a better day out: a walking pilgrimage with songs and a picnic in a garden.

practice: Think of two churches you could reach in one afternoon: two, not seven, and they don't have to be grand.
Picture a minute in the first, then the stretch between, a bench or a café where you'd eat, and who might come along; Philip walked in a crowd.
If you pray, say one Our Father in each; if you don't, sit a minute in each and notice what's different.

wordCard.voice: The seven churches of Rome. A one-day walking pilgrimage to seven great churches, which Philip Neri made joyful with songs and a shared lunch. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: pilgrims with a picnic. In Philip's walk, lunch on the grass was part of the prayer. Until tomorrow.
